en: I spoke with my mom yesterday.
note: Completed past: hablar → hablé with yo. Ayer sets the event yesterday.
Completed past: llegar → llegaste with tú. The regular tú ending is -aste.
Completed past: comprar → compró with él. The accent distinguishes compró from compro.
Llamó is a completed past action. Me, the person called, goes before the verb.
Trabajamos can be present or completed past. Ayer makes the past meaning clear.
Completed past: comer → comieron with ellos. Regular -er and -ir verbs share -ieron here.
Completed past: salir → salieron with ustedes, the plural you.
Terminé presents finishing as a completed event. The -é ending identifies yo.
Entender → entendí in the completed past. It does not use the present-tense ie here.
Dormir → dormiste with tú in the completed past. No explicit tú is needed.
Fui is the yo completed-past form of ir. It also belongs to ser; context tells you which verb.

en: We went to the movies on Saturday.
note: Ir → fuimos with nosotros. El sábado refers to a particular Saturday here.
Estuvo presents her stay here as a bounded past event. Estar describes location.
Tener has the irregular completed-past stem tuv-: tuve with yo.
Hacer → hizo with él in the completed past. Notice the z in hizo.
Ver → vimos. Use the personal a before a specific person: a tu hermana.

es: Le di las llaves a él.
note: Dar → di. Le marks the recipient, and a él makes him explicit.
Decir has the irregular form dijeron with ellos. It ends in -eron, not -ieron.

en: I put the bag on the table.
es: Puse la bolsa en la mesa.
note: Poner has the irregular completed-past stem pus-: puse with yo.

en: You came with your family. (one person)
note: Venir → viniste in the completed past. Tú is the subject; tu means your.
Traer has the irregular completed-past form trajo with ella.
Poder → pude. No pude ir describes being unable to go on that occasion.

en: We had to wait an hour.
note: Tener que expresses obligation. Tuvimos places it in a completed past situation.
Encontrar → encontré in the completed past; it does not use ue in this form.
Perder → perdió with él. Su refers to his here because of the context.
Pagar → pagaron with ustedes in the completed past.
Olvidar → olvidé. Tu without an accent means your.
Aprender → aprendimos in the completed past. Algo nuevo means something new.
Leer → leyó with ella. Notice the y in this completed-past form.
Regular -ir verbs use -í with yo in the completed past: escribir → escribí.
Abrir → abrieron with ellos in the completed past.

en: I woke up at six today.
es: Hoy me desperté a las seis.
note: Despertarse → me desperté. The reflexive pronoun stays before the conjugated verb.
Llovió describes a completed period of rain. Weather verbs usually have no personal subject.
Hubo is the completed-past form of impersonal hay. It stays singular, even with multiple events.

es: La película terminó a las diez.
note: Terminó marks the movie's ending as a completed event.
Habitual/background past: vivía describes a former living situation. Antes means before or formerly.

en: You used to work on Sundays. (one person)
note: The imperfect trabajabas describes a past routine. Los domingos means on Sundays.

en: She used to walk to school.
note: The imperfect caminaba can describe what someone used to do regularly.

en: We used to eat together every day.
note: Comíamos is the imperfect nosotros form. Todos los días makes the repeated habit clear.

en: They used to play in the park.
note: Jugaban describes a past habit. Jugar does not use ue in the imperfect.

en: You used to come every summer. (plural)
note: Venían is the imperfect form for ustedes. Cada verano signals a repeated past action.

en: When I was a child, I had a dog.
es: Cuando era niño, tenía un perro.
note: Era and tenía describe a past life stage and situation. A female speaker can say cuando era niña.

en: We used to go to the beach in summer.
es: Íbamos a la playa en verano.
note: Ir has the irregular imperfect form íbamos with nosotros.
Hacía describes a recurring past action here. Siempre reinforces the habit.
Sabía describes a past state of knowledge. No sabía means I didn't know in this context.
Hacía frío uses the imperfect to describe the weather as background.

en: There were a lot of people at the party.
es: Había mucha gente en la fiesta.
note: Había describes what was present. Gente is grammatically singular even though it means people.

en: I was cooking when you called. (one person)
note: Estaba cocinando gives the ongoing background; llamaste marks the completed call during it.

en: She was sleeping when I arrived.
note: Dormir → durmiendo after estar. Estaba gives the ongoing background; llegué is the arrival.

en: We were tired after the trip.
note: Estábamos describes a past state. An all-female group can say estábamos cansadas.
